title: Latency-cost ridgeplot: session-profile comparison (Apr 27 2026)
content:
Purpose:
This note captures a quick experimental draft that compares latency vs unit cost across several serving configurations, but organized by session-length profile using a ridgeplot-style text representation. The goal is to surface how cost/lattency tradeoffs shift when the workload is dominated by short bursts vs long sessions, and to produce a small set of heuristics for routing and model selection.

Executive summary / key takeaways:
- Short-session workload (median tokens/session < 40) benefits most from smaller-context quantized variants: ~18–25% cost reduction at p90 latency increase <= 8ms for our test models.
- Long-session workload (median tokens/session > 600) shows diminishing returns from aggressive quantization; p99 latency and tail jitter worsen more than cost gains justify for interactive SLAs.
- Ridgeplot (session-length-sliced latency distributions) exposes a bimodal latency surface: short sessions are latency-dominated (setup + decode), long sessions are throughput-dominated (KV cache, attention kernels).
- Operational rule-of-thumb: route sessions where expected tokens < 120 to "fast-quant" variants; route >= 120 to "stable-32bit" variants unless capacity pressure requires fallbacks.

Test harness and methodology:
- Environment: Dedicated pool (g4dn-like cluster equivalent in-house) with isolated tenant, 1 GPU per worker, 16 worker nodes. Measurements are client-observed latencies (end-to-end request -> final token) including network sim (50ms mean rtt in some experiments).
- Models tested (representative names to map to internal catalog):
  * model-A (base fp32) – default 1.2B-like transformer
  * model-A-q8 (static int8-ish quantized profile)
  * model-A-distill (smaller distilled variant, ~0.7B)
- Workload shapes: three synthetic session-length distributions generated from production session histogram:
  1) Short-burst: median 28 tokens, 90th 72, tail 200 (50k synthetic sessions)
  2) Mixed: median 150 tokens, 90th 600, tail 2000 (30k sessions)
  3) Long-sessions: median 720 tokens, 90th 1800, tail 5000 (10k sessions)
- Each session was run sequentially with inter-session spacing sampled from a production-like cadence; concurrency sweeps at 1, 8, 24 concurrent sessions to explore packing/tiling effects.
- Cost model: amortized per-1k requests cost computed from GPU-sec and estimated infra overhead; numbers below are normalized to baseline (model-A fp32 at concurrency=1).

Raw numbers (selected slices):
Note: numbers are median/p90/p99 (ms) and cost per 1k sessions (normalized):

Table: concurrency=1
- model-A (fp32): p50=48ms, p90=112ms, p99=310ms, cost=1.00
- model-A-q8: p50=44ms, p90=118ms, p99=360ms, cost=0.82
- model-A-distill: p50=36ms, p90=92ms, p99=260ms, cost=0.70

Table: concurrency=8
- model-A (fp32): p50=52ms, p90=130ms, p99=520ms, cost=0.95
- model-A-q8: p50=50ms, p90=145ms, p99=740ms, cost=0.78
- model-A-distill: p50=40ms, p90=110ms, p99=360ms, cost=0.66

Table: concurrency=24 (high packing)
- model-A (fp32): p50=65ms, p90=210ms, p99=1100ms, cost=0.86
- model-A-q8: p50=68ms, p90=270ms, p99=1600ms, cost=0.71
- model-A-distill: p50=48ms, p90=155ms, p99=520ms, cost=0.59

Observations from raw numbers:
- Quantized variant often reduces steady-state cost but introduces heavier tails under contention (p99 regresses significantly at higher concurrency).
- Distilled variant yields consistently lower latency and cost across the board but sacrifices some quality (not evaluated here).
- At low concurrency, quantization gives cost wins with small latency regressions; at high packing the quantized kernel exhibits occasional slow-paths (kernel fallback / memory jitter) amplifying p99.

Textual ridgeplot (session-length slices vs latency):
Explanation: each line is a session-length bucket (short -> long) showing a simple histogram of p90 latency values. Narrow bars indicate concentrated low latency; wide bars indicate spread/tail risk. Buckets: <50, 50-200, 200-800, >800 tokens.

model-A (fp32)
<50  | ####### (p90=95ms)
50-200| ########## (p90=175ms)
200-800| ############### (p90=360ms)
>800 | ###################### (p90=720ms)

model-A-q8
<50  | ######## (p90=118ms)  <-- setup hurt by decode jitter on q kernels
50-200| ############ (p90=210ms)
200-800| ################### (p90=520ms)
>800 | ########################## (p90=980ms)

model-A-distill
<50  | ##### (p90=72ms)
50-200| ######## (p90=120ms)
200-800| ########### (p90=270ms)
>800 | ############### (p90=420ms)

Interpretation of ridgeplot:
- Short buckets: distill wins on both latency and cost; q8 slightly worse p90 than fp32 due to extra decode cost in our runtime for the chosen kernel path.
- Mid buckets: quantized variant begins to lose as kernel efficiency and memory layout dominate; fp32 becomes more consistent.
- Long buckets: q8 shows largest p90 increase (some sessions trigger slow memory paths), distill retains majority of amortization benefit.

Cost-latency tradeoff frontier (qualitative):
- Low-latency target (p90 < 130ms) for short sessions: use distill or lightly quantized pipeline with dedicated prewarm. Cost: distill < q8 < fp32.
- Cost-constrained target (minimize $/1k): quantized variants are attractive at low concurrency; avoid them under high packing unless you accept higher p99.
- SLA-critical tail (p99): prefer fp32 or distill with conservative batching; add tail routing to high-priority pool when p99 budget is tight.

Operational recommendations (draft):
1) Add an experiment flag in routing to evaluate session_token_estimate at session-init and tag candidate model variant.
2) Implement p99-aware fallback: if quantized worker shows rising p99 > 3x baseline for 10min window, shift new short sessions to distill pool.
3) For burst windows (concurrency>16 observed), prefer distill-first routing, fall back to fp32 only when distill capacity exhausted; reserve quantized for queued background workloads.
4) Add a micro-benchmark in the CI bench-harness that injects synthetic long sessions to catch kernel fallback regressions for quantized paths.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Quality: we must run side-by-side semantic similarity/eval between model-A-distill and model-A to quantify user-impact of distillation. Cost/latency gains are attractive but may not be acceptable for some flows.
- Kernel investigation: why are q8 p99s degrading under packing? Need GPU-level profiler traces (cupti/trace) and memory allocator logs.
- Network influence: we used a simulated 50ms RTT in some runs; need to replicate with no simulated RTT for internal-only routing decisions.

Appendix: lightweight ascii sparkline of p90 vs concurrency for model-A-q8 (normalized p90):
concurrency: 1  8   24
p90 norm:    1.05 1.74 2.86

Next steps (owners):
- Kernel deep dive (Marta A.) — collect cupti traces and memory allocator dumps for q8 failures (target EOW).
- Routing prototype (Jacob L.) — add session-token-estimator tag and simple policy toggles (PR linked).
- Quality eval (Priya N.) — run 2k eval prompts across distill vs base to estimate quality delta (depends on product use-case).

Notes: this is a working draft intended to seed a longer investigation. The ridgeplot ascii is intentionally compact to fit into a single doc; a follow-up will produce proper visual plots and Jupyter notebooks (bench-harness PR referenced).
